Learning Objectives
Discuss the role of radiation therapy in patients with soft-tissue sarcoma.
List the indications and contraindications for radiation therapy in patients with soft-tissue
sarcoma.
Describe the differences between preoperative and postoperative radiation therapy in
patients with soft-tissue sarcoma.
Explain the complications of radiation therapy in patients with soft-tissue sarcoma.
Review the outcomes associated with neoadjuvant and adjuvant radiation therapy in patients
with soft-tissue sarcoma


Although surgical resection remains the cornerstone in the management of localized
soft-tissue sarcoma (STS), the use of radiation therapy as part of the multimodal local
control strategy is well supported by the literature compared with the role of
chemotherapy, which is less clear. The routine use of radiation therapy in the
management of high-grade STS has allowed for a very high rate of limb-sparing surgery
(LSS) while maintaining acceptable oncologic outcomes.
Background and Basic Information
Background
Before the introduction of radiation therapy for extremity STS, amputation was considered the
standard therapeutic procedure to achieve local control. Early in the history of STS therapy, the
role of radiation therapy was to eliminate microscopic residual disease from areas outside the
tumor pseudocapsule. With the routine implementation of radiation therapy, surgeons can
excise the tumor with closer margins, thereby sparing critical structures and allowing for limb
salvage, with resultant maximization of functional outcomes without compromise of oncologic
outcomes.1
The local management of STS generally includes surgery with or without radiation therapy.
Radiation therapy may include external beam radiation therapy (EBRT), image-guided intensity
modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), or brachytherapy.
Basic Information
Irradiation is a physical agent used to destroy cancer cells. The irradiation used is called
ionizing irradiation because it forms ions (electrically charged particles) and deposits energy in
the cells of the tissues through which it passes. High-energy irradiation may lead to DNA
damage, impeding the ability of cells to divide and proliferate further2,3 (Resource 1).
Radiation therapy can be used in combination with other treatment modalities, such as
surgery, chemotherapy, or immunotherapy. If used preoperatively (neoadjuvant therapy),

irradiation will kill tumor cells outside of the margin that may be responsible for recurrence. If
used postoperatively (adjuvant therapy), irradiation will destroy microscopic tumor cells that
may have been left behind.4
Irradiation can be delivered to the location of the cancer via two methods. EBRT is delivered
from outside the body by aiming high-energy rays (photons or particle radiation) to the
location of the tumor. Internal irradiation or brachytherapy is delivered from inside the body
via radioactive sources sealed in catheters or seeds placed directly into the tumor site.5
Indications/Rationale
Reduces Local Recurrence
Radiation therapy is a key aspect of the multimodal management of high-grade STS.
Radiation therapy in combination with wide excision of localized STS decreases local
recurrence.

Reduces Local Recurrence
Two randomized controlled studies have established the role of radiation therapy in limb
salvage resection and decreasing local recurrence. In 1982, the National Cancer Institute
(NCI) I trial established adjuvant radiation therapy as an integral component of
multimodal limb conservation STS management. In this trial by Rosenberg et al,6
patients were randomized to wide excision with radiation therapy or amputation. The
study findings showed no significant differences in disease-free survival rates (71% and
78% at 5 years; P = 0.75) or overall survival rates (83% and 88% at 5 years; P = 0.99)
between the limb-sparing group and the amputation group.6 In the 1990s, a NCI II
randomized clinical trial by Yang et al7 evaluated adjuvant radiation therapy with
conservative surgical resection versus surgical resection alone. All patients with high-
grade lesions underwent chemotherapy. At a mean follow-up of 9.6 years, overall local
control rates were 99% in the radiation therapy and surgical resection group compared
with 77% in the surgical resection alone group. Local recurrence was substantially
associated with the absence of radiation therapy.

Role in Unplanned Excision
Unplanned excisions create considerable difficulties in the management of STS.
Unplanned excisions often require additional surgical management with wide excision of the
tumor bed.
Radiation therapy often is used in management of unplanned excisions.

Role in Unplanned Excision
Surgical management of a presumed benign soft-tissue mass without appropriate
preoperative imaging studies or biopsy followed by excision of the lesion without
attention to surgical margins is not uncommon. Such surgical management is termed an
unplanned excision.8 Unplanned excision of STS is a cause of potential morbidity
because of the need for additional management. If salvage management is performed at
a sarcoma center with considerable experience, oncologic outcomes may be acceptable;
however, unplanned excision may result in increased morbidity from more complex soft-
tissue reconstruction after tumor bed excision and, in some situations, amputation.
Although the benefits of radiation therapy have been established in management of
localized STS, the role of radiation therapy is not as well defined in patients who undergo
unplanned excision. In a retrospective review of 78 patients who underwent unplanned
excision, Kepka et al9 reported local failure after radiation therapy in only 9 patients
(12%); however, several studies have shown radiation therapy alone to be ineffective in
preventing local recurrence after unplanned excisions.10,11 Overall retrospective data
favor a combined strategy of radiation therapy and tumor bed excision in most patients
who undergo unplanned excisions.9 In patients in whom tumor bed excision is medically
or anatomically prohibitive, radiation therapy alone may be an alternative salvage
treatment option.
Role After Resection

4/37

In patients in whom final pathologic assessment results in microscopically positive margins or
margins deemed inadequate, a boost of postoperative radiation therapy has been suggested.
No evidence suggests that outcomes are improved with a postoperative boost.

Role After Resection
The role of additional radiation therapy in the form of postoperative EBRT in patients
with positive margins after preoperative radiation therapy remains unproven for local
control and may subject patients to additional toxicity and long-term complications. A
2014 retrospective cohort study by Pan et al12 showed that the use of a radiation
therapy boost in extremity STS after preoperative radiation therapy and resection with
positive margins did not enhance local control. Five-year local control rates were 100%
for no boost, 78% for brachytherapy/intraoperative radiation therapy, and 71% for EBRT
(postoperative boost) (P = 0.5). In patients who receive preoperative radiation therapy
and have positive margins at the time of surgical treatment, a multidisciplinary
discussion should be held regarding the role of additional surgical management for
wider margins or the role of additional radiation therapy for local control.12
Role in an Inoperable Tumor
In patients with an inoperable sarcoma, radical radiation therapy has been assessed in many
retrospective studies using photons or proton therapy.13,14
In radical radiation therapy for inoperable tumors, a standard practice is to deliver doses
higher than 66 Gy, leading to a local control rate of 25% to 50%, depending on tumor type and
grade.15
Contraindications and Specific Considerations
Superficial Sarcomas and Stage I Disease

Wide-margin surgical excision alone may be adequate for smaller, superficial, and low-grade
tumors.

Superficial Sarcomas and Stage I Disease
Based on the lower risk of local recurrence, National Comprehensive Cancer Network
guidelines have recommended surgical excision alone for small T1 (=5.0 cm) high-grade
sarcomas and low-grade sarcomas for which wide margins can be attained.16 In a
prospective trial, Pisters et al17 evaluated surgical resection alone of localized,
nonmetastatic, T1 (=5.0 cm) primary STS of the extremity or superficial trunk with only
selective use of radiation therapy. The authors reported an acceptable rate of local
control (local recurrence, 7.9% at 5 years) and excellent long-term survival (3.2% rate of
sarcoma-specific death at 5 years) in patients treated via R0 resection (ie, no microscopic
tumor at the inked margin) alone and who, therefore, may be spared the short- and
long-term toxicities associated with radiation therapy
Location-Specific Considerations
The risk of complications with radiation therapy may be increased in some anatomic locations.

Location-Specific Considerations
The likelihood of toxicity after definitive radiation therapy depends, at least partially, on
the size and location of the tumor, factors that affect the amount and type of healthy
tissue exposed to higher doses. The incidence of major complications that may result
from radiation therapy in the definitive setting varies based on the site managed;
however, complications may include soft-tissue necrosis, fibrosis, neuropathy, bone
fracture, and bowel injury.18

Rohde et al19 reported complications in 19 of 26 patients (73%) with a STS of the hand
who were treated via EBRT and/or brachytherapy (preoperatively or postoperatively),
with a median follow-up of 7 years. Complications developed in 3 of the 29 patients
treated via surgery alone s. The authors observed that brachytherapy near the
metacarpophalangeal joints may result in severe functional disability and likely is best
avoided in this location. Complications include metacarpophalangeal joint ankylosis,
tendon adhesion requiring surgical tenolysis, and joint contractures.
Schoenfeld et al20 also described the effect of radiation therapy on local control of distal
upper and lower extremity STSs. Of the 23 patients in their series, who were evaluated
over 26 years, 12 had lesions of the hand and wrist and 11 had lesions of the foot. The
late effects of radiation therapy in these patients included edema (14%), fibrosis (24%),
telangiectasia (24%), hyperpigmentation (19%), impaired range of motion (33%), and
impaired functional use of the extremity (14%).
Patient Age and Comorbidities
Older age and decreased functional status may decrease radiation therapy tolerance and
increase complications.

Patient Age and Comorbidities
Comorbidities and functional deficits may increase with age; however, clinical and
preclinical data suggest that chronologic age is not correlated with healthy tissue
tolerance. Most of the retrospective data on radiation therapy alone do not show
considerable differences between older patients without comorbidities who are in good
performance status and younger patients.21 Combinations of radiation therapy and
chemotherapy increase acute effects, and elderly patients are more vulnerable to toxic
effects of treatment.22 A specific geriatric assessment is crucial to determine which
patients are candidates for radiation therapy.23,24

Histologic-Specific Considerations
Atypical Lipomatous Tumors
Radiation therapy rarely is used for atypical lipomatous tumors (also known as well-
differentiated liposarcomas) except in patients with difficult-to-manage recurrent disease.

Atypical Lipomatous Tumors
Most studies have shown that the role of radiation therapy in the primary treatment of
patients with atypical lipomatous tumors/well-differentiated liposarcomas is not
associated with a decreased time to recurrence.17,25,26 Radiation therapy does appear
to be associated with decreased recurrence if administered to patients with recurrent
disease; therefore, it should be reserved for these patients.25 One study showed that
marginal resection (R1) resulted in an acceptable local recurrence rate in 3 of 31 patients
(7.5%) with an atypical lipomatous tumor.27
Extraskeletal Ewing Sarcoma
The rarity of extraskeletal Ewing sarcoma EES precludes determination of any benefit of the
use of adjuvant radiation therapy in patients treated surgically; however, current
recommendations are for treatment via the same protocols as those for skeletal Ewing
sarcoma. Therefore, localized EES is managed via chemotherapy and surgery or radiation
therapy for local control.16

Extraskeletal Ewing Sarcoma
Based on data from the National Cancer Database (NCDB), Saiz et al28 evaluated the role
of radiation therapy in the management of adults with EES who were treated via surgery
and chemotherapy. The authors reported that the addition of radiation therapy in
patients with localized EES managed via chemotherapy and surgical resection did not
result in any considerable improvement in overall survival. Local recurrence data are not

8/37

available in the NCDB; therefore, the effect of radiation therapy on local control could
not be determined. Some studies have advocated for the use of adjuvant radiation
therapy in patients who have EES with local recurrence or poor histologic response to
chemotherapy.29 In a more recent institutional study at MD Anderson Cancer Center,
the possible benefit of combined-modality local therapy (surgery and radiation therapy)
over single-modality local therapy (surgery or radiation therapy) was evaluated in the
management of localized EES. Sixty patients with EES were evaluated; one-half of the
patients were treated via combined-modality local therapy, and all patients underwent
chemotherapy. In this cohort, combined-modality local therapy did not result in an
improved local control rate (ie, no local recurrence; 83% for combined-modality local
therapy versus 72% for single-modality local therapy; ;0.41).30
Myxoid/Myxoid Round Cell Liposarcoma
Myxoid liposarcoma has a particular sensitivity to RT.

Myxoid/Myxoid Round Cell Liposarcoma
Radiotherapy has a significant role in preventing local relapse, reducing tumor size, and
improving microscopic margin status in patients with myxoid liposarcoma/round cell
liposarcoma. A retrospective study evaluating 418 cases (311 patients with myxoid
liposarcoma and 107 with myxoid round cell liposarcoma; > 5% round cell)
demonstrated an overall 10-year local control rate of 93% after surgical resection and RT,
but RT did not affect survival. Radiotherapy was effective in preventing local
recurrence.31
Myxofibrosarcoma
Myxofibrosarcoma is known to cause particular challenges with regard to surgical margins and
recurrence.


Myxofibrosarcoma
Myxofibrosarcoma is one of most common sarcomas in elderly adults, and, in most
patients, it arises in the extremities. Because of their infiltrative patterns,
myxofibrosarcomas require large resection with frequent reconstructive surgery. Data
support that radiation therapy in combination with surgical treatment should be used in
patients with myxofibrosarcoma. After R0 resection, adjuvant radiation therapy should
be delivered; after R1 resection (R1 = microscopically positive margins), scar re-excision
and adjuvant radiation therapy should be discussed.32 Ghazala et al33 found that
microscopic tumor may be present as far as 29 mm from the macroscopic tumor in
patients with a fascially based tumor. Given the infiltrative nature of myxofibrosarcoma,
assessment of the tumor margin is unreliable. In addition, the size of the tumor in
patients with negative margins was not significantly different from the size of the tumor
in patients with positive margins (9.5 cm versus 8.5 cm, respectively; P = 0.6). In planning
for radiation therapy after resection of tumor, regardless of the tumor margin, the entire
tumor and the adjacent potentially involved tissues should be included because of the
characteristic extensive infiltrative nature of myxofibrosarcoma.
Timing, Dosing and Duration, and Techniques
Sequencing (Preoperative Versus Postoperative)
Radiation therapy can be administered preoperatively or postoperatively with good local
control outcomes.
Because of the risks of long-term complications, most sarcoma centers advocate for
preoperative radiation therapy.

Sequencing (Preoperative Versus Postoperative)
Although the delivery of radiation therapy in patients with a large and/or high-grade
extremity sarcoma is considered standard, considerable controversy existed regarding
the timing of delivery of radiation therapy relative to surgical management. Preoperative

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000562
10/37

radiation therapy permits the radiation therapy oncologist to deliver a lower irradiation
dose (typically 50 Gy versus 66 to 70 Gy delivered in the adjuvant setting) to a smaller
target volume (preoperative extent with margin versus entire surgical bed with margin),
potentially minimizing late toxicity. In addition, marginally resectable tumors may
sufficiently respond to preoperative radiation therapy to allow for negative margin
functional resection.34 Evidence has shown that if radiation therapy is administered in a
neoadjuvant, multidisciplinary fashion, critical structures (ie, blood vessels, nerves, bone)
occasionally may be spared without compromising local recurrence outcomes.35
Radiation therapy may be delivered postoperatively rather than preoperatively for
various reasons, including the postoperative diagnosis of sarcoma, upgrading after
evaluation during surgical management, failure to attain a negative margin with
acceptable functional outcomes, and more extensive lesion than expected based on
preoperative imaging studies and pathologic data. If radiation therapy is delivered
postoperatively, at least 5 cm of margin is included, and a dose of 60 Gy or higher is used
because the dose of radiation therapy delivered in the postoperative setting has been
shown to correlate with local control.36
A landmark trial involved randomization between preoperative and postoperative
radiation therapy. The results showed equivalent local control outcomes between
preoperative and postoperative radiation therapy; however, wound complications were
higher in the preoperative radiation therapy group for tumor size larger than 5 cm (35%
versus 17%) than in the postoperative radiation therapy group. Long-term complications
(eg, edema, stiffness) were higher in the postoperative radiation therapy group because
of a higher dose and a larger field.37.
Treatment Planning
The management of STS is determined by a multidisciplinary treatment group and ideally at
centers with considerable sarcoma experience.
Treatment planning includes consideration of dosing, timing, anticipated margins, and location
of critical structures.


Treatment Planning
For radiation therapy delivered preoperatively, a discussion with the surgeon may help
avoid high-dose regions in areas destined to be incision or drain sites, potentially
decreasing wound complications. In addition, the sarcoma surgeon and the radiation
therapy oncologist can anticipate and plan for margins that are close to critical
structures.35 In general, radiation therapy oncologists attempt to exclude sensitive
structures—uninvolved compartments, joint spaces, genitalia, and visceral organs—from
the irradiation field to minimize toxicity. CT and MRI provide complementary information
for radiation therapy planning and should be performed if possible.38
In the postoperative setting, radiopaque surgical clips placed at the time of resection
may help delineate the tumor bed and the area at high risk to help facilitate targeting
these areas with radiation therapy. In the preoperative or postoperative setting,
surgeons must protect uninvolved compartments of the limb from receiving the full dose
to spare lymphatics. Typically, the radiation therapy plan also is optimized to reduce the
dose to poorly vascularized areas, such as the pretibial, prepatellar, and preolecranon
skin.38.
Dosing and Typical Treatment Duration
The typical preoperative radiation therapy dose is 50 Gy administered over 25 sessions (5
weeks).
The postoperative radiation therapy dose is 60 to 66 Gy administered over 30 to 33 days.
Delayed postoperative radiation therapy of more than 4 months results in poorer outcomes.

Dosing and Typical Treatment Duration
FPreoperative EBRT generally involves a dose of 50 Gy to the tumor (with a margin to
include microscopic disease), divided into 25 fractions of 2 Gy and administered over 5
weeks. A postoperative boost of radiation therapy consisting of an additional 16-Gy dose

12/37

can be administered; however, this has not been found to improve local control and is
associated with postoperative complications. Postoperative radiation therapy is initiated
4 to 6 weeks postoperatively, after adequate wound healing has been documented.
Radiation therapy typically is administered over a 30- to 33-day course for a total dose of
60 to 66 Gy. The higher dose of radiation therapy is needed because of the tissue
hypoxia observed in a surgical wound bed; in addition, the treatment volume is larger to
include the entire surgical field (ie, to cover every area of potential contamination
because of surgical management).38
A retrospective study of 100 patients by Schwartz et al39 showed that delayed
postoperative radiation therapy of more than 4 months was associated with inferior
local control rates (5-year local relapse–free survival, 62%) for intermediate- and high-
grade STSs of the extremity and torso.
Techniques and Modalities
Multiple radiation therapy modalities have been used in the management of STS3,40 (Resource
2).
Radiation therapy in patients with STS can be administered preoperatively (neoadjuvant),
intraoperatively, or postoperatively (adjuvant) via EBRT or brachytherapy using radioactive
isotopes.
Target Volumes
The target for preoperative radiation therapy should be delineated as follows (Figure 1):

Figure 1 Axial (A) and sagittal (B) CT scans of a posterior left thigh with soft-tissue sarcoma
show preoperative radiation therapy volumes. Gross tumor volume is shown in red, clinical
target volume is shown in blue, and planning target volume is shown in pink. (Reproduced
from Ahmed SK, Owen D: Radiation therapy, in Biermann JS, Siegel G, eds: Orthopaedic

Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2021, pp 83-96.)
The gross tumor volume (GTV) is defined as the gross demonstrable location and extent of
tumor. It is determined based on gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted MRIs. In addition to the
primary site, gross tumor involving lymph nodes or spread into adjacent tissues should be
included in the GTV.41
The clinical target volume (CTV) is defined as demonstrable GTV plus margin of subclinical
disease spread and constructed by expanding the GTV by 3 to 4 cm longitudinally and 1.5 cm
laterally and anteroposteriorly. The CTV should include peritumoral edema observed on T2-
weighted MRIs but should not be expanded beyond the surface of the adjacent bones, fascia,
and skin unless these structures are involved.40,41
The planning target volume is defined as the CTV with anisotropic margins to account for
possible uncertainties in beam alignment, patient positioning, organ motion, and organ
deformation.42

The CTV is extended in all directions by 1.5 cm, except longitudinally, in which expansion is 4
cm. Radially, the CTV should include the scar and any postoperative fluid collection but does
not need to be expanded further than the skin and the surface of the adjacent bones, fascia,
and joints, unless these structures are involved.43
External Beam Radiation Therapy
Three-Dimensional Conformal Radiation Therapy
Traditionally, EBRT techniques for preoperative or postoperative management used parallel
opposed pair of treatment beams
Three-dimensional conformal radiation therapy or image-guided IMRT currently is used.

Three-Dimensional Conformal Radiation Therapy
The parallel opposed pair plan is associated with the advantages of simplicity and
reproducibility of setup and homogeneous dose to the tumor, with less likelihood of
geographic mass; however, conformity is poor, and excessively high radiation doses are
delivered to more of the surrounding healthy tissue than necessary. A combination of
three or more beams, typical of three-dimensional conformal radiation therapy and
IMRT, reduces the extent of healthy tissues receiving the prescribed target dose.44.
Image-Guided IMRT
Image-guided IMRT also has been widely used in patients with STSs.

Image-Guided IMRT
This technique allows for better control over the treatment field and dose, with
improvement in sparing nearby healthy tissues and critical structures, such as
bone, vessels, nerves, and skin (Figure 2). The use of IMRT also has resulted in
improvements in local tumor control and a reduction in many complications
associated with radiation therapy compared with historical EBRT techniques.45
In a nonrandomized study, local control with IMRT was considerably better than

Particle Radiation Therapy
EBRT also is performed with the use of heavier particles, such as neutrons, protons,
and heavy ions (helium, carbon, and nitrogen).
Protons can offer better dose distribution because of their unique absorption profile
in tissues.
Deposition of maximum destructive energy at the tumor site while minimizing
damage to healthy tissues along their path

Particle Radiation Therapy
To date, no randomized studies have compared particle radiation therapy with
photons in sarcoma management. The superior dose distribution and improved

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000562
16/37

conformity of protons in combination with better sparing of healthy tissue have
been offered as an argument for implementing particle radiation therapy,
particularly in patients with rare tumors, such as sarcomas, and in children in
whom the risk of late secondary cancer is of particular concern.48,49
Brachytherapy
Brachytherapy provides local radiation to the tumor bed via radioactive seeds or
catheters.
Good outcomes have been shown with this modality; however, in general, it has been
implemented much less often than EBRT/IMRT.

Brachytherapy
Brachytherapy involves the delivery of local irradiation to a tumor bed via
radioactive seeds or catheters placed at the time of surgical management. The
catheters are placed at regular intervals and oriented perpendicular or parallel
to the incision during surgical management; accurate catheter placement is
critical to create a precise treatment field (Figure 3). Brachytherapy is initiated
shortly after surgery, with radiation therapy infusion for a total of 5 days.
Brachytherapy can be used in isolation or in combination with traditional EBRT
techniques as a potential boost to the surgical bed without the delay in
treatment associated with a postoperative boost of EBRT. Improved local
control has been reported with a combination of brachytherapy and EBRT
rather than with brachytherapy alone.50

Complications
Radiation therapy is associated with acute and long-term complications.
Acute complications include wound healing complications, infection, and edema.
Long-term complications include fibrosis, stiffness, fracture, edema, and secondary
malignancies.

Complications

Although the choice of neoadjuvant versus adjuvant radiation therapy is considered on
an individualized patient basis, most studies have demonstrated equivalent disease
control;37,51 however, considerable differences in toxicity profiles exist between these
two approaches. In general, neoadjuvant radiation therapy is associated with more acute
wound complications, whereas adjuvant radiation therapy is associated with higher rates
of late toxicity and decreased limb function.52 Current guidelines favor neoadjuvant
radiation therapy because of the reduced irradiation dose and volumes, thereby
reducing the cumulative exposure of healthy tissues to radiation therapy. Table 1 lists a
summary of the incidence of complications from radiation therapy.52-57

Wound Complications
Preoperative radiation therapy results in increased wound complications after surgical
resection.


Wound Complications
Radiation therapy and chemotherapy are believed to inhibit wound healing, presumably
by preventing collagen synthesis (Figure 4). Even without preoperative radiation therapy,
wound healing complications commonly occur after resection of extremity STS, with
rates reported to be as low as 6% to as high as 42%.58 A trial by O’Sullivan et al37
confirmed that preoperative radiation therapy is associated with higher wound
complication rates (35%) than postoperative radiation therapy (17%); tumor size and
anatomic site also were substantial risk factors.
Figure 4 Photograph of the posterolateral distal thigh of a 50-year-old man shows
wound dehiscence after neoadjuvant radiation therapy and surgical resection of
rhabdomyosarcoma. (Courtesy of Dr. R. Lor Randall, FACS, Sacramento, CA.)
Large dead spaces; devascularization of remaining tissue; and long, thin, undermined
surgical flaps used to close the wound can contribute to delayed wound healing. Surgical
wounds created in the absence of adjuvant therapy may require 2 or more years for the
reparative process to be completed and may only reach 80% of maximum tensile
strength compared with uninjured tissue.59

The risks of wound complications can be minimized by timing surgical management at 4
to 6 weeks after the completion of radiation therapy and via the judicious use of soft-
tissue flaps for wound closure and incisional vacuum-assisted closure dressings.60 A
prospective study by O’Sullivan et al61 indicated that image-guided IMRT may ameliorate
the risk and severity of wound complications by reducing the dose to the tissues to be
used for wound closure after STS resection.
Edema
Chronic lymphedema is another potential source of morbidity that may arise from radiation
therapy for STS of the extremity.

Edema
The higher the dose of radiation therapy delivered, and the greater the extent of the
limb irradiated, the higher the risk for considerable chronic lymphedema. Stinson et al53
found that 19% of patients treated postoperatively via 60 to 65 Gy experienced
lymphedema that was grade 2 or greater in severity. Davis et al55 reported that 15% of
patients treated via preoperative radiation therapy and 23% of patients treated via
postoperative radiation therapy experienced grade 3 or greater lymphedema.
Joint Stiffness/Fibrosis
Joint contracture and fibrosis that follow radiation therapy may lead to impairments in long-
term limb function or decreased mobility.

Joint Stiffness/Fibrosis
Contracture is considerably more common if more than 50% of the affected joint is
irradiated.55 In a prospective clinical trial, Stinson et al53 assessed the late effects of

of patients reported tissue induration, 20% experienced joint contracture, and 32%
experienced decreased range of motion in the managed extremity.
Fracture
Another serious potential late radiation therapy–related complication is fracture.

Fracture
Radiation therapy–associated fractures (Figure 5) are difficult to manage and rarely heal
despite appropriate reduction and fixation. They may result in substantial morbidity,
often requiring replacement with the use of a megaprosthesis. Prognostic factors for
fracture of the irradiated bone included periosteal stripping as part of resection of the
tumor, administration of chemotherapy, and femalesex.54 In a large series of patients
treated via surgery and radiation therapy for a lower extremity STS, Holt et al62 reported
that high-dose radiation therapy (60 or 66 Gy) was associated with a higher risk of bone
fracture than lower doses (50 Gy) of radiation therapy delivered to the extremity.

Chronic neuropathy and associated pain are rare occurrences for patients treated via radiation
therapy in combination with surgery for STS. This late complication also is associated with
higher doses of radiation therapy.

Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
Stinson et al53 reported that 7% of patients treated via doses between 60 and 65 Gy
experienced pain that required narcotic agents, and that a higher dose (>63 Gy) was a
substantial predictor of chronic pain. Strength or sensory deficit resulting from
irradiation-induced nerve damage is more rare, with rates of less than 1% reported in
one study.52
Irradiation-Induced Sarcoma
Irradiation-induced sarcomas (RISs) represent a very small subset of sarcomas that are linked
to previous radiation therapy. They are associated with a more aggressive biology and poorer
outcomes.

Irradiation-Induced Sarcoma
The 10-year cumulative risk for RIS after radiation therapy is estimated to be 0.03% to
0.8%.63 Genetic factors, young age at the time of treatment, and high-dose radiation
therapy with simultaneous use of chemotherapy with alkylating agents are considered
risk factors for RIS.64 In a Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results data-based study,
the incidence and relative risk of RIS was evaluated. Breast cancer was associated with
the highest risk for RIS after radiation therapy compared with other solid tumors. The
incidence of RIS after radiation therapy for the management of primary extremity STS
was not specifically reported.65
RIS is associated with a relatively long latency period after initial radiation therapy ,
ranging from 3 months to 55 years (median, 14 years).66 The most commonly reported

Oncologic and Functional Outcomes
Local Recurrence
Local recurrence represents a combination of treatment failure and a potentially aggressive
biology.
Local recurrence is related to microscopic resection margin, tumor location, locally recurrent
presentation, patient age, histopathologic subtype, tumor size, and tumor grade.69
The use of radiation therapy has been shown to substantially reduce local recurrence after LSS
in patients with extremity STS.

Local Recurrence
The use of radiation therapy for deep-seated, high-grade sarcoma is supported by two
NCI randomized studies showing that limited LSS in combination with adjuvant radiation
therapy results in acceptable oncologic outcomes compared with amputation and lower
local recurrence rates than LSS alone.6,7 Other studies also have supported these
findings. In a systematic review and meta-analysis involving 11 studies, Albertsemeier et
al70 demonstrated that EBRT reduced local recurrence in 3,155 patients with a STS in an
extremity, the head/neck, or a truncal location (odds ratio, 0.49; P = 0.001).
In a multicenter retrospective study, Willeumier et al71 evaluated the effect of surgical
margins and radiation therapy in a multistate model. In this cohort of 687 patients with a
high-grade STS from four orthopaedic oncology referral centers, wide surgical margins
and radiation therapy decreased local recurrence. The hazard ratio for postoperative
radiation therapy was 4.36 (95% confidence interval, 1.34 to 14.24; P = 0.015) and the

Overall Survival
Radiation therapy primarily is indicated to decrease the risk of local recurrence in limb
salvage/function-preserving surgical resection and, therefore, is not necessarily thought to
play a role in improving overall survival.

Overall Survival
In the development of a nomogram that combines the factors to predict the probability
of 12-year sarcoma-specific death, the independent factors that affected disease-specific
survival were tumor grade, tumor size, tumor site, histopathology, patient age, and
resection margins.72 Tumor grade, size, and histopathology exerted their effect largely
via their influence on metastatic recurrence, whereas, tumor site, patient age, and
resection margins exerted their effect via predisposition to local recurrence. In a long-
term follow-up of the NCI II trial, Beane et al73 reported no improvement in survival in
patients in the EBRT plus LSS group.
In an NCDB study, Gingrich et al74 identified 27,969 patients with a STS of an extremity
who underwent surgical resection. The authors observed that a negative surgical margin
and preoperative or postoperative radiation therapy were associated with improved
overall survival in patients with low-grade or high-grade sarcoma.74
Margins
The goal of the surgical management of extremity STS is excision with wide margins.
The use of radiation therapy has allowed for close margins to save critical structures and
preserve function while maintaining acceptable local recurrence outcomes.

Radiation therapy in itself cannot make up for inadequate margins or poor treatment

Margins
The NCDB study by Gingrich et al74 demonstrated that preoperative radiation therapy
independently predicted higher rates of R0 resection; the rates of R0 resection for
preoperative radiation therapy, postoperative radiation therapy, and no radiation
therapy cohorts were 90.1%, 74.9%, and 79.9%, respectively (P < 0.001).
Grade
Radiation therapy primarily is indicated for high-grade sarcoma.
Radiation therapy also may be indicated in the management of low-grade sarcoma in patients
with a large tumor or in patients in whom management of local recurrence may be worse than
the complications associated with radiation therapy.

Grade
The efficacy of postoperative EBRT after LSS was demonstrated in a prospective
randomized study (91 patients with high-grade sarcoma and 51 patients with low-grade
sarcoma). Postoperative radiation therapy considerably reduced the 10-year local
recurrence rate among the patients with a high-grade lesion: no local recurrence in
patients who underwent LSS and EBRT versus 21% in patients who underwent surgical
treatment alone (P = 0.0028). Among patients with low-grade sarcoma (after excluding
patients with desmoid tumors or dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans), the recurrence
rates were 5% and 32% for LSS and EBRT versus LSS alone, respectively (P = 0.016).7

completely resected STS of the extremity or the superficial trunk were randomized
intraoperatively to undergo brachytherapy or not undergo brachytherapy, with a median

Functional Outcomes
The goal of limb salvage is to achieve acceptable local control results (ie, low risk of local
recurrence) while maximizing functional outcomes.
Limb-preserving resection in combination with radiation therapy have drastically improves
functional outcomes compared with amputation.

Functional Outcomes
Patients treated radiation therapy and LSS have good overall functional outcomes. In a
20-year follow-up study of the NCI II randomized controlled trial on LSS versus LSS and
EBRT,7 Beane et al73 reported that the group treated via LSS and EBRT had good
functional outcomes, with 88% able to ambulate and independently perform activities of
daily living. In addition, only 8% of patients in that group required an assistive device to
ambulate.
A prospective observational study aimed to investigate changes in objectively measured
functional outcomes in 29 patients with an extremity STS within the first year after LSS.75
The study investigated the association between functional outcomes, based on the
Toronto Extremity Salvage Score and the Musculoskeletal Tumor Society Score, and
objective measures of functional outcomes, including isokinetic dynamometry. The study
reported transient decreases in Toronto Extremity Salvage Scores and Musculoskeletal
Tumor Society Scores in the months postoperatively; however, scores improved at 1 year
postoperatively (median Toronto Extremity Salvage Score at baseline and 1 month, 2
months, and 1 year postoperatively, 96.5, 78.5, 88, and 88, respectively). Radiation
therapy had no effect on functional outcomes in this study. The muscle strength of the

In most patients, LSS in combination with radiation therapy results in improved
functional outcomes compared with amputation; however, it is associated with a
substantial risk for acute and long-term adverse effects. Previous studies, including one
by Bell et al,1 reported good functional outcomes. In a multivariate analysis, tumor size
and intraoperative neural sacrifice were considerable predictors of functional outcomes.
Poor results included limb weakness from nerve destruction and fractures, which mainly
were observed in the proximal thigh and the shoulder girdle. Approximately 50% of
patients resumed full employment.1
The technique and location of radiation therapy also are important in predicting or
determining functional outcomes. In a study by Stinson et al,53 joint contracture was
predicted by joint inclusion in the irradiation field. Strength deficit and swelling were
predicted by the size of the irradiation field and by anatomic location in the lower
extremity. Several studies have reported a correlation between total dose (higher than
55 Gy) and skin fibrosis and functional outcomes.76,77
Summary

Summary
STSs of the extremity are a heterogeneous group that require a multidisciplinary
treatment approach. Considerable progress has been made in defining the benefits and
risks of radiation therapy and the timing of radiation therapy (preoperative versus
postoperative). Improvements in surgical and radiation therapy modalities and
techniques lead to improved function-preserving LSS. Research is ongoing to address a
number of concerns. including the timing and dosing/fractionation of irradiation, the

Attempts to improve the local control benefit achieved via radiation therapy while
minimizing toxicity have led to the use of highly conformal therapies. In some patients,
surgical treatment alone may yield acceptable outcomes to avoid radiation therapy–
related complications; regardless, these decisions should be made in a multidisciplinary
setting and in a patient- and tumor-specific manner.
